## Code Status

Runs end to end. Renamed from `tone_assignment_methods.qmd` on 2026-11-17; last rendered
under that name on 2026-11-11 with no errors (`tone_assignment_methods.html`).
Feeds Section 7.7 of the capstone write-up.

## Purpose

The first-round comparison of tone assignment methods. Every method family is scored
**in-sample**: the tones a method keeps are chosen from the same ratings it is scored on, so
the results are optimistic. The held-out comparisons are in `methods_heldout.qmd` and
`methods_candidates.qmd`.

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: Setup
options(conflicts.policy = "depends.ok")
library(tidyverse)
plot_grid <- cowplot::plot_grid
source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/blob/main/format_path.R?raw=true")
source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/blob/main/fun_eda.R?raw=true")
source("https://github.com/jjcurtin/lab_support/blob/main/fun_plots.R?raw=true")
source(here::here("scripts", "functions_llmpanel.R"))

path_processed <- format_path("llmpanel/data_processed")

# Read in and format the panel in long format (one row per message rating)
panel_long <- format_eda(read_csv(
  here::here(path_processed, "panel.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE), long = TRUE)

# tone_levels (the five tones) is defined in functions_llmpanel.R

# Each respondent's mean rating for each of the 5 tones, ignoring style.
# (Ratings are averaged across formal and informal messages)
tone_means <- panel_long |>
  summarise(rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(subid, tone))
```

# Introduction

This script will detail various tone assignment methods in competition with
each other as the most optimal strategy for personalizing support messages.
The differentiation between these methods relies on a unique balance of
two factors:

- Maximizing message helpfulness. Our leading principle is an
assumption that increases in self-reported helpfulness may translate to
improved efficacy of support messages. The 'mean-only' method, for instance,
would assign the singular tone that was rated highest on average across the
whole sample to each participant indiscriminately.

-- We also have two unique performance metrics that expand from message
   helpfulness and provide additional insight into how equitable each
   assignment method is:
   
--- Rate of Optimization: For each method, how often would a user receive a
    message from their highest-rated tone(s)? Averaged across the sample.
    
--- Rate of Disadvantage: For each method, how often would a user receive a
    message from their lowest-rated tone(s)? Averaged across the sample.
    
  We can imagine that two methods may have equivalent mean helpfulness, but one
  will have improved rates of Optimization or Disadvantage that ensure fewer
  users are on the negative end of a deployed method's bias. 
  
  Candidate methods will follow a checklist: Satisfying mean helpfulness within
  an acceptable range, minimizing disadvantage, then maximizing optimization.
  The other consideration is:

- Retaining variability in tone. Users who receive support messages on a daily
schedule may develop fatigue if they encounter the same tone repeatedly. If we
alternate higher-rated and lower-rated tones in-vivo, this may help to prevent
any specific tone from losing efficacy over time. Methods in this script will
range from maximum to minimum amounts of variability, which can be viewed as a
trade-off with mean message helpfulness, as well as rates of optimization and
disadvantage.

Our goal is to determine what amount of variability may be required to
maintain optimal message efficacy, and at what point may we begin to experience
diminishing returns with variability where an increase in consistency with
higher-rated tones would be more beneficial.

## A Note on Style

Style (formal vs. informal) is ignored throughout this script. Tone effects did
not meaningfully depend on style (the tone-by-style interaction was very small,
and individuals showed no differences in their tone-by-style pattern), so every
tone is evaluated using each respondent's ratings of that tone averaged across
formal and informal messages. Because formal messages were rated about 0.13
points lower on average, absolute helpfulness here is slightly pessimistic
relative to informal-only delivery. Both shifts affect all methods
similarly, so the comparison between methods is the focus.

# Benchmarking

No tone received 'perfect' 7/7 ratings from every single participant, which
means that we have a natural limit to how far we can improve message helpfulness
through any method. Let's look at our best and worst case scenarios in terms of
message helpfulness:

## Worst-Case Method (Every user gets their lowest-rated tone only)
```{r}
#| label: Worst-Case Method
# This code takes the panel data and identifies for each
# user the tone(s) with the lowest mean rating.
# (averaged across the 3 formal and 3 informal messages in that tone)

# Tied tones are kept in worst_tone_1 : worst_tone_4
# (NA when there is no tie that large)
panel_worst <- extreme_tones_wide(tone_means, min, "worst_rating", "worst_tone")
attr(panel_worst, "label") <- "Worst case"
attr(panel_worst, "fill") <- "firebrick"

plot_rating_hist(panel_worst, "worst_rating",
                 "Worst-case: each respondent's lowest-rated tone",
                 fill = "firebrick")
```

## Best-Case Method (Every user gets their highest-rated tone only)
```{r}
#| label: Best-Case Method
# This code takes the panel data and identifies for each
# user the tone(s) with the highest mean rating.

# Tied tones are kept in best_tone_1 ... best_tone_4
panel_best <- extreme_tones_wide(tone_means, max, "best_rating", "best_tone")
attr(panel_best, "label") <- "Best case"
attr(panel_best, "fill") <- "forestgreen"

plot_rating_hist(panel_best, "best_rating",
                 "Best-case: each respondent's highest-rated tone",
                 fill = "forestgreen")
```

To be clear, we are unable to deploy this best-case method in-vivo as we will
only have data from the preferences survey and demographics to make tone
assignments. This distribution assumes that for our sample, the assignment
method ended up producing a perfect result with maximum attainable helpfulness.

```{r}
#| label: Best vs Worst Case
# Best-case (top) and worst-case (bottom) distributions stacked on the same scale.
compare_methods(top = panel_worst, bot = panel_best)
```

Here we can see a substantial difference between our best and worst-case
scenarios, suggesting further that tone really does matter. Our contender
methods for in-vivo assignment will attempt be produce results that are
comparable to the best-case distribution while retaining some reasonable amount
of variability.

# Baseline Methods

## Uniform Variability (All Tones)

On the maximum variability end, our default method would be to use all tones in
equal proportion. There are two primary justifications for this approach:

- We run the lowest risk of any particular tone losing efficacy over time if
all tones are used equally often.

- If we are unsure about which tones may be better than others for a particular
user, we ought not reduce or eliminate the presence of any particular tone.

```{r}
#| label: Uniform Variability
# This code chunk will create a histogram that shows the distribution of each
# respondent's mean message rating across all tones (ignoring style).

panel_uniform <- tone_means |>
  summarise(uniform_rating = mean(rating), .by = subid)
attr(panel_uniform, "label") <- "Uniform variability"
attr(panel_uniform, "fill") <- "grey60"

plot_rating_hist(panel_uniform, "uniform_rating",
                 "Uniform variability: each respondent's mean across all tones")
```

## Mean-Only Assignment

On the no-variability end, our default method would be to use the single tone
that was rated highest on average across the whole sample. In-vivo, this means
that every user would receive the exact same tone regardless of their
self-reported preferences.

```{r}
#| label: Mean-Only Assignment
# This code chunk will identify the tone that was rated highest on average
# across the whole sample.
# Then, a df 'panel_mean' will be created, that contains a single column with the mean message rating for each individual user for that same tone.
#'panel_mean' will be used to create a histogram that includes the mean and standard deviation within the plot.

# Tone with the highest mean rating across the whole sample
tone_sample_means <- tone_means |>
  summarise(mean_rating = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE), .by = tone) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_rating))
tone_sample_means

best_tone <- tone_sample_means$tone[1]

# Readable label, e.g. "Self efficacy"
best_tone_label <- best_tone |>
  str_replace_all("_", " ") |>
  str_to_sentence()

panel_mean <- tone_means |>
  filter(tone == best_tone) |>
  select(subid, mean_only_rating = rating)
attr(panel_mean, "label") <- paste0("Mean-only (", best_tone_label, ")")
attr(panel_mean, "fill") <- "darkorange"

plot_rating_hist(panel_mean, "mean_only_rating",
                 paste0("Mean-only: everyone receives ", best_tone_label),
                 fill = "darkorange")
```

```{r}
# Compare baselines with best-case
compare_methods(top = panel_uniform, mid = panel_mean, bot = panel_best)
```

Both baseline methods are already comparable to the best-case method, with the
uniform variability method theoretically benefitting from 

```{r}
#| label: Worst-Case Tone Counts
# Each respondent's worst-case tone: tone-level mean rating (averaged across
# formal and informal), then the lowest-rated tone(s). Ties count once per tied tone.
worst_tone_counts <- tone_means |>
  filter(near(rating, min(rating)), .by = subid) |>
  count(tone, name = "n_respondents", sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(pct_of_respondents = n_respondents / n_distinct(tone_means$subid))

worst_tone_counts
```

Here we see ~18% of respondents are receiving their worst-case tone with the
mean-only method. This is quite problematic if we consider almost 1/5 users
being disadvantaged as much as possible. We are also sacrificing all variability
with this approach, which raises our concern about helpfulness declining even
among those who most preferred the mean format.

# Simple Exclusion Methods

Using sample-wide patterns in the data, we can exclude the tones which were
generally lower-rated, and least likely to be someones highest-rated. While we
sacrifice some variability with each tone being removed, we can hope to still
gain many benefits over a single tone assignment method.

## 2-Tone Variability (Value Affirmation & Self-Efficacy)

These two tones were the highest rated on average. This method would restrict
variability for all users to an alternating pattern of support messages written
in both tones. Performance for this method will be estimated by averaging user
ratings across both tones.

```{r}
#| label: 2-Tone Variability (VA & SE)
# This code chunk will calculate the average message rating
# for each user across the "value affirmation" and "self efficacy" tones
# combined.
# Then, a df 'panel_2tone' will be created, that contains a single column with
# the mean message rating for each individual user across the combination of
# those two tones.

panel_2tone <- panel_long |>
  filter(tone %in% c("value_affirmation", "self_efficacy")) |>
  summarise(two_tone_rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = subid)
attr(panel_2tone, "label") <- "2-tone (Value affirmation & Self efficacy)"
attr(panel_2tone, "fill") <- "steelblue"
```

```{r}
# Compared with uniform variability and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_uniform, mid = panel_2tone, bot = panel_best)
```

This method moves mean helpfulness closer to the best-case distribution,
with a slight spike in the left-hand tail. Some users will have had their
highest-rated tone removed with this method, however the majority of users did
not rate those tones highly and are benefiting as a result.

```{r}
#| label: Disadvantaged by 2-tone
# How many users disadvantaged by 2tone
```

## 3-Tone Variability (Value Affirmation, Self-Efficacy, Legitimizing)

This method adds the 3rd highest rated tone on average, introducing a bit more
variability at the potential cost of immediate message helpfulness.
Performance for this method will be estimated by averaging user
ratings across all 3 tones.

```{r}
#| label: 3-Tone Variability (VA, SE, LE)
# This code chunk will calculate the average message rating
# for each user across the "value affirmation", "self efficacy" and 
# 'legitimizing' tones combined.
# Then, a df 'panel_3tone' will be created, that contains a single column with
# the mean message rating for each individual user across the combination of
# those 3 tones.

panel_3tone <- panel_long |>
  filter(tone %in% c("value_affirmation", "self_efficacy", "legitimizing")) |>
  summarise(three_tone_rating = mean(rating_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = subid)
attr(panel_3tone, "label") <- "3-tone (Value affirmation, Self efficacy & Legitimizing)"
attr(panel_3tone, "fill") <- "mediumpurple"
```

```{r}
# Compared with uniform variability and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_uniform, mid = panel_2tone, bot = panel_3tone)
```

As expected, the 3-tone method moves us slightly back away from the best-case
distribution, however we have flattened the left-hand tail in comparison to
the 2-tone distribution. Less users are disadvantaged this way, and the impact
on mean helpfulness is marginal.

It should be noted that both of these simple exclusion methods remain very
similar to uniform variability with only small improvements in mean helpfulness.

# Method Summary

Each method is scored on its mean helpfulness (and the SD across respondents)
and on two exposure metrics that describe how often respondents actually see
their best and worst tones. Kept tones are shown in equal proportion unless the
method specifies weights.

- **weighted_opt:** the average proportion of a respondent's messages written in their highest-rated tone(s). If tones are tied for highest, messages in any of them count. For example, with the 30/30/20/10/10 weighting, someone whose top tone is Self efficacy has a weighted_opt of .30.
- **weighted_dis:** the average proportion of messages written in the respondent's lowest-rated tone(s), with the same tie rule.

Respondents tied across all five tones have every tone as both highest and lowest, so they contribute 1 to both metrics. Uniform variability uses every tone, the mean-only method uses only the sample's highest-rated tone, and the best-case and worst-case benchmarks use only each respondent's own highest- or lowest-rated tone. Add a row for any new method with `track_method()`.

```{r}
#| label: Method Tracker
# Every tied tone is used, in equal proportion
kept_best <- tied_tones_long(panel_best, "best_tone")
kept_worst <- tied_tones_long(panel_worst, "worst_tone")

method_tracker <- NULL |>
  track_method(panel_worst, kept_worst) |>
  track_method(panel_uniform, tone_levels) |>
  track_method(panel_mean, best_tone) |>
  track_method(panel_2tone, c("value_affirmation", "self_efficacy")) |>
  track_method(panel_3tone, c("value_affirmation", "self_efficacy", "legitimizing")) |>
  track_method(panel_best, kept_best)

method_tracker
```

# Weighted Methods

Up until now, our methods with variability have been evaluated under an
assumption that tones will be used in equal proportion to one another. This 
section considers alternate versions of these methods where users can have a
rank order that leads a user to see certain retained tones more often than
others. This demonstration with the weighted version of the uniform variability
method will help to explain:

## Uniform Weighted (30/30/20/10/10)

```{r}
# This chunk will create a new object 'panel_uniform_weighted' that takes the
# weighted average of a users message ratings according to this formula:
# .30(self efficacy) + .30(value affirmation) + .20(legitimizing) + .10(norms)
# + .10(acknowledging)

tone_weights <- c(self_efficacy = .30, value_affirmation = .30, legitimizing = .20,
                  norms = .10, acknowledging = .10)
stopifnot(all.equal(sum(tone_weights), 1),
          setequal(names(tone_weights), tone_levels))

# Weighted mean of each respondent's tone-level ratings (weights rescaled by the
# weights actually present, in case a tone rating is missing)
panel_uniform_weighted <- tone_means |>
  mutate(weight = tone_weights[tone]) |>
  summarise(weighted_rating = sum(weight * rating) / sum(weight), .by = subid)
attr(panel_uniform_weighted, "label") <- "Weighted variability (30/30/20/10/10)"
attr(panel_uniform_weighted, "fill") <- "darkcyan"

plot_rating_hist(panel_uniform_weighted, "weighted_rating",
                 "Weighted variability: primary and secondary tones weighted by rank",
                 fill = "darkcyan")

# Compared with equal-proportion uniform variability and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_uniform, mid = panel_uniform_weighted, bot = panel_best)
```

## 3-Tone Weighted (40/40/20)

The 3-tone method with its tones shown unequally: Self efficacy and Value
affirmation (the two highest-rated tones) each make up 40% of messages, and
Legitimizing makes up 20%.

```{r}
#| label: 3-Tone Weighted
tone_weights_3 <- c(self_efficacy = .40, value_affirmation = .40, legitimizing = .20)
stopifnot(all.equal(sum(tone_weights_3), 1))

panel_3tone_weighted <- tone_means |>
  filter(tone %in% names(tone_weights_3)) |>
  mutate(weight = tone_weights_3[tone]) |>
  summarise(weighted_3tone_rating = sum(weight * rating) / sum(weight), .by = subid)
attr(panel_3tone_weighted, "label") <- "3-tone weighted (40/40/20)"
attr(panel_3tone_weighted, "fill") <- "slateblue"

plot_rating_hist(panel_3tone_weighted, "weighted_3tone_rating",
                 "3-tone weighted: Self efficacy 40%, Value affirmation 40%, Legitimizing 20%",
                 fill = "slateblue")

# Compared with the equal-proportion 3-tone method and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_3tone, mid = panel_3tone_weighted, bot = panel_best)
```

### 3-Tone Weighted: Alternative Weight Sets

The same three tones with the primary tones (Self efficacy and Value affirmation,
weighted equally) given more or less of the messages. Five sets are compared: 35/35/30,
37.5/37.5/25, 40/40/20 (above), 42.5/42.5/15, and 45/45/10. The third number is
Legitimizing's share.

```{r}
#| label: 3-Tone Weighted Sweep
sweep_weights <- list(
  "35/35/30" = c(self_efficacy = .35, value_affirmation = .35, legitimizing = .30),
  "37.5/37.5/25" = c(self_efficacy = .375, value_affirmation = .375, legitimizing = .25),
  "42.5/42.5/15" = c(self_efficacy = .425, value_affirmation = .425, legitimizing = .15),
  "45/45/10" = c(self_efficacy = .45, value_affirmation = .45, legitimizing = .10))
stopifnot(all(map_dbl(sweep_weights, sum) == 1))

panels_3tone_sweep <- imap(sweep_weights, \(w, nm) {
  weighted_method(
    expand_grid(subid = unique(tone_means$subid),
                tibble(tone = names(w), weight = unname(w))),
    label = paste0("3-tone weighted (", nm, ")"), fill = "slateblue",
    rating_name = "weighted_3tone_rating")
})

# From the most even weighting (top) through 40/40/20 (middle) to the most uneven (bottom)
compare_methods(top = panels_3tone_sweep[["35/35/30"]], mid = panel_3tone_weighted,
                bot = panels_3tone_sweep[["45/45/10"]])

# Track the new weight sets (40/40/20 is tracked below)
for (nm in names(sweep_weights)) {
  w <- sweep_weights[[nm]]
  method_tracker <- track_method(method_tracker, panels_3tone_sweep[[nm]], weights = w)
}
method_tracker
```

```{r}
#| label: Weighted Method Tracker
# Add the two fixed-weight methods (30/30/20/10/10 and 40/40/20) to the tracker
method_tracker <- method_tracker |>
  track_method(panel_uniform_weighted, weights = tone_weights) |>
  track_method(panel_3tone_weighted, weights = tone_weights_3)

method_tracker
```

# Simple Individualized Exclusion

Up until now, we have made generalization about the sample as a whole, with
each assignment method applying the same tone exclusions universally across
all participants. Methods in this section will leverage data from the tone
preferences survey to personalize which tones are excluded.

## Drop Least-Preferred Tone

This method eliminates the least-preferred tone(s) according to the tone
preferences survey, and assigns the remaining 1-4 tones in equal proportion.

```{r}
# For each respondent, identify which tone(s) were lowest on the preferences
# survey, and remove the corresponding message ratings. Average message ratings
# across the remaining tone(s) and use that for the new 'panel_drop_low' object.

# Each respondent's preference score for each tone (from the preferences survey)
pref_by_tone <- panel_long |>
  distinct(subid, pref_legitimizing, pref_norms, pref_value_affirmation,
           pref_self_efficacy, pref_acknowledging) |>
  pivot_longer(-subid, names_to = "tone", names_prefix = "pref_", values_to = "pref")

# Tones kept after dropping the lowest-preferred tone(s). All tones tied for lowest
# are dropped together; a respondent who rated every tone the same keeps all five.
kept_drop_low <- drop_least_preferred(pref_by_tone, n_drop = 1)

panel_drop_low <- tone_means |>
  semi_join(kept_drop_low, by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
  summarise(drop_low_rating = mean(rating), .by = subid)
attr(panel_drop_low, "label") <- "Drop least-preferred tone"
attr(panel_drop_low, "fill") <- "indianred"

plot_rating_hist(panel_drop_low, "drop_low_rating",
                 "Drop least-preferred tone(s): mean rating across remaining tones",
                 fill = "indianred")

# Tones remaining per respondent
kept_drop_low |> count(subid) |> count(n, name = "respondents")

# Compared with uniform variability and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_uniform, mid = panel_drop_low, bot = panel_best)
```

## Drop Two Tones

This method eliminates the 2 least-preferred tones according to the tone
preferences survey, and assigns the remaining tones in equal proportion.

```{r}
# For each respondent, identify which 2 tones were lowest (5th and 4th place)
# on the preferences survey, and remove the corresponding message ratings.
# Average message ratings across the remaining tone(s) and use that for the new
# 'panel_drop_two' object.
# If there was a 2-way tie at the bottom, drop only those 2 and keep 3 left
# If there was a 3-way tie at the bottom, drop those 3 and keep 2 left
# If there was a 4-way tie at the bottom, keep only the top-preferred tone.
# (A tie that straddles the cutoff is dropped together, and a respondent who rated
# every tone the same keeps all five.)

kept_drop_two <- drop_least_preferred(pref_by_tone, n_drop = 2)

panel_drop_two <- tone_means |>
  semi_join(kept_drop_two, by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
  summarise(drop_two_rating = mean(rating), .by = subid)
attr(panel_drop_two, "label") <- "Drop two least-preferred tones"
attr(panel_drop_two, "fill") <- "goldenrod"

plot_rating_hist(panel_drop_two, "drop_two_rating",
                 "Drop two least-preferred tones: mean rating across remaining tones",
                 fill = "goldenrod")

# Tones remaining per respondent
kept_drop_two |> count(subid) |> count(n, name = "respondents")

# Compared with dropping only the least-preferred tone and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_drop_low, mid = panel_drop_two, bot = panel_best)
```

```{r}
#| label: Individualized Exclusion Tracker
# Add the two individualized exclusion methods to the tracker
method_tracker <- method_tracker |>
  track_method(panel_drop_low, kept_drop_low) |>
  track_method(panel_drop_two, kept_drop_two)

method_tracker
```

## Weighted individualized Exclusion

```{r}
# This method sorts each respondent's preference survey into 1-5 tiers from
# highest to lowest preference rating. Respondent's with a 2-way tie at the
# bottom will have only 4 tiers, for instance.
# Message ratings will then be weighted appropriately based upon how many tiers
# their preferences sort into, and how many messages per tier, and the preference
# ratings themselves. For instance, tones with a preference rating of 7 should be
# seen 1/6 more often than tones rated at a 6, and so on.
#
# Implementation: each tone's weight is (preference score - 1) divided by the sum of
# (preference score - 1) across that respondent's five tones, so tied tones get equal
# weights (a tier with more tones is shown more in total), a tone at the scale
# minimum is never shown, and a respondent with every tone at the minimum gets equal
# weights. Each respondent's method rating is the weighted mean of their tone ratings.

weights_individual <- preference_weights(pref_by_tone, offset = 1)

panel_weighted_indiv <- tone_means |>
  inner_join(weights_individual, by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
  summarise(weighted_indiv_rating = sum(weight * rating), .by = subid)
attr(panel_weighted_indiv, "label") <- "Weighted individualized (preference - 1)"
attr(panel_weighted_indiv, "fill") <- "mediumseagreen"

plot_rating_hist(panel_weighted_indiv, "weighted_indiv_rating",
                 "Weighted individualized: tones weighted by preference score - 1",
                 fill = "mediumseagreen")

# Number of preference tiers per respondent (tied tones share a tier)
pref_by_tone |>
  drop_na(pref) |>
  summarise(n_tiers = n_distinct(pref), .by = subid) |>
  count(n_tiers, name = "respondents")

# Compared with uniform variability and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_uniform, mid = panel_weighted_indiv, bot = panel_best)
```

```{r}
#| label: Weighted Individualized Tracker
# Add the preference-weighted method to the tracker
method_tracker <- method_tracker |>
  track_method(panel_weighted_indiv, weights = weights_individual)

method_tracker
```

## Tier-Weighted Individualized

A sharper version of the weighted method that uses only the order of each
respondent's preferences. Tones are sorted into preference tiers (tied tones
share a tier), and each tier is shown half as often as the tier above it: tier 1
twice as often as tier 2, four times as often as tier 3, and so on. Tied tones
each get their tier's weight. Unlike the previous method, the size of the
preference gaps does not matter, only the ranking.

```{r}
#| label: Tier-Weighted Individualized
weights_tier <- tier_weights(pref_by_tone, ratio = 2)

panel_tier_weighted <- tone_means |>
  inner_join(weights_tier, by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
  summarise(tier_weighted_rating = sum(weight * rating), .by = subid)
attr(panel_tier_weighted, "label") <- "Tier-weighted individualized (1:1/2:1/4...)"
attr(panel_tier_weighted, "fill") <- "orchid"

plot_rating_hist(panel_tier_weighted, "tier_weighted_rating",
                 "Tier-weighted individualized: each tier shown half as often as the one above",
                 fill = "orchid")

# Compared with the preference-score weighting and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_weighted_indiv, mid = panel_tier_weighted, bot = panel_best)

method_tracker <- method_tracker |>
  track_method(panel_tier_weighted, weights = weights_tier)

method_tracker
```


## Power-Weighted Individualized

A sharper version of the preference-score weighting. Each tone's weight is
proportional to (preference score - 1) raised to a power, so the weighting
becomes steeper toward the most-preferred tones as the power grows, while still
respecting the size of the gaps between scores. A power of 1 is the earlier
`pref - 1` method. Set `power_weight` to tune it.

```{r}
#| label: Power-Weighted Individualized
power_weight <- 2

weights_power <- preference_weights(pref_by_tone, offset = 1, power = power_weight)

panel_power_weighted <- tone_means |>
  inner_join(weights_power, by = c("subid", "tone")) |>
  summarise(power_weighted_rating = sum(weight * rating), .by = subid)
attr(panel_power_weighted, "label") <- paste0("Power-weighted individualized (power = ", power_weight, ")")
attr(panel_power_weighted, "fill") <- "tomato"

plot_rating_hist(panel_power_weighted, "power_weighted_rating",
                 paste0("Power-weighted individualized: weight proportional to (preference - 1)^",
                        power_weight),
                 fill = "tomato")

# Compared with the unpowered preference weighting and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_weighted_indiv, mid = panel_power_weighted, bot = panel_best)

method_tracker <- method_tracker |>
  track_method(panel_power_weighted, weights = weights_power)

method_tracker
```


## Weighted Methods With Dropped Tones

Each of the three weighted methods (preference-score, tier, and power weighting)
is repeated after first dropping the least-preferred tone (drop low) or the two
least-preferred tones (drop two), using the same tie rules as the simple
exclusion methods. The weights are then computed among the tones that remain.

```{r}
#| label: Weighted Methods With Dropped Tones
# Preference scores for the tones kept after each drop
prefs_drop_low <- semi_join(pref_by_tone, kept_drop_low, by = c("subid", "tone"))
prefs_drop_two <- semi_join(pref_by_tone, kept_drop_two, by = c("subid", "tone"))

# Preference-score weighting (pref - 1)
panel_weighted_indiv_low <- weighted_method(
  preference_weights(prefs_drop_low, offset = 1),
  "Weighted individualized + drop low", "mediumseagreen", "weighted_indiv_low")
panel_weighted_indiv_two <- weighted_method(
  preference_weights(prefs_drop_two, offset = 1),
  "Weighted individualized + drop two", "mediumseagreen", "weighted_indiv_two")

# Tier weighting (each tier half as often as the one above)
panel_tier_weighted_low <- weighted_method(
  tier_weights(prefs_drop_low, ratio = 2),
  "Tier-weighted + drop low", "orchid", "tier_weighted_low")
panel_tier_weighted_two <- weighted_method(
  tier_weights(prefs_drop_two, ratio = 2),
  "Tier-weighted + drop two", "orchid", "tier_weighted_two")

# Power weighting ((pref - 1)^power)
panel_power_weighted_low <- weighted_method(
  preference_weights(prefs_drop_low, offset = 1, power = power_weight),
  "Power-weighted + drop low", "tomato", "power_weighted_low")
panel_power_weighted_two <- weighted_method(
  preference_weights(prefs_drop_two, offset = 1, power = power_weight),
  "Power-weighted + drop two", "tomato", "power_weighted_two")

# Each weighting with no drop (top), drop low (middle), and drop two (bottom)
compare_methods(top = panel_weighted_indiv, mid = panel_weighted_indiv_low,
                bot = panel_weighted_indiv_two)
compare_methods(top = panel_tier_weighted, mid = panel_tier_weighted_low,
                bot = panel_tier_weighted_two)
compare_methods(top = panel_power_weighted, mid = panel_power_weighted_low,
                bot = panel_power_weighted_two)

method_tracker <- method_tracker |>
  track_method(panel_weighted_indiv_low, weights = preference_weights(prefs_drop_low, offset = 1)) |>
  track_method(panel_weighted_indiv_two, weights = preference_weights(prefs_drop_two, offset = 1)) |>
  track_method(panel_tier_weighted_low, weights = tier_weights(prefs_drop_low, ratio = 2)) |>
  track_method(panel_tier_weighted_two, weights = tier_weights(prefs_drop_two, ratio = 2)) |>
  track_method(panel_power_weighted_low,
               weights = preference_weights(prefs_drop_low, offset = 1, power = power_weight)) |>
  track_method(panel_power_weighted_two,
               weights = preference_weights(prefs_drop_two, offset = 1, power = power_weight))

method_tracker |> arrange(desc(mean)) |> arrange(weighted_dis) |> arrange(desc(weighted_opt))
```


## Tuning the Weighted Methods

Each individualized weighted method has one setting that controls how sharply
the preferences are weighted, and each can be run with no drop, dropping the
least-preferred tone, or dropping the two least-preferred tones:

- **Weighted individualized:** weights proportional to (preference - offset). A larger
  offset removes more of the lowest-scoring tones, and a large negative offset
  approaches an even distribution.
- **Tier-weighted:** each tier is shown `ratio` times as often as the next tier down.
  A ratio of 1 is an even distribution.
- **Power-weighted:** weights proportional to (preference - 1) raised to a power.
  Smaller powers flatten the weighting.

Only the range where weighting stays gentle enough is considered: the least-seen tone
must be delivered at least `min_share` (10%) of the time, for at least
`min_respondents` (half) of respondents, all the way up to an even distribution
(20% per tone, or an even split among the tones left after a drop). The least-seen
tone is the one with the smallest weight among the tones the method delivers, so a
tone the weighting pushes to 0% counts as 0. Edit `tuning_settings` to try other
values. All results are in `weight_tuning`, and only configurations that meet the
minimum are added to `method_tracker`.

```{r}
#| label: Weighted Method Tuning
min_share <- 0.10       # least-seen tone must be delivered at least this often...
min_respondents <- 0.50 # ...for at least this share of respondents

# Settings run from sharp to an even distribution (offset very negative, ratio = 1)
tuning_settings <- bind_rows(
  tibble(family = "Weighted individualized", param = c(-6, -3, -1, 0, 1, 2)),
  tibble(family = "Tier-weighted", param = c(1, 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3)),
  tibble(family = "Power-weighted", param = c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)))

weight_tuning_grid <- tuning_settings |>
  cross_join(tibble(drop = c("none", "low", "two")))

weight_tuning <- tune_weighted_methods(
  weight_tuning_grid, pref_by_tone, kept_drop_low, kept_drop_two, min_share = min_share) |>
  mutate(drop = factor(drop, levels = c("none", "low", "two"),
                       labels = c("No drop", "Drop low", "Drop two")),
         meets_min = pct_meets_min >= min_respondents)

weight_tuning |>
  select(family, param, drop, mean, sd, weighted_opt, weighted_dis,
         min_share_median, pct_meets_min, meets_min)

# Add the configurations that meet the minimum to the tracker (rows with the same
# method name are replaced)
tuning_in_range <- filter(weight_tuning, meets_min)

method_tracker <- method_tracker |>
  filter(!method %in% weight_tuning$method) |>
  bind_rows(select(tuning_in_range, method, mean, sd, weighted_opt, weighted_dis))

# Settings left out for dropping the least-seen tone below the minimum
weight_tuning |> filter(!meets_min) |> count(family, drop, name = "configurations_excluded")

method_tracker
```

```{r}
#| label: Weighted Method Tuning Plot
# Tuning plot: each metric against the tuning setting, one column per method family and
# one line per drop option. The dashed line is the minimum share for the least-seen tone.
metric_labels <- c(mean = "Mean helpfulness",
                   weighted_opt = "Share in highest-rated tone(s)",
                   weighted_dis = "Share in lowest-rated tone(s)",
                   min_share_median = "Least-seen tone share (median respondent)")

weight_tuning |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(names(metric_labels)), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = names(metric_labels), labels = metric_labels)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = param, y = value, color = drop)) +
  geom_hline(data = tibble(metric = factor(metric_labels[["min_share_median"]],
                                           levels = metric_labels),
                           yintercept = min_share),
             aes(yintercept = yintercept), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(metric ~ family, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Tuning setting (offset, ratio, or power)", y = NULL, color = NULL,
       subtitle = "Dashed line = minimum share for the least-seen tone")
```

# Data-Driven Method

This method drops Acknowledging for everyone, since it was among the lowest-rated
tones overall, then uses each respondent's preferences among the remaining four tones
(sorted into 1 to 4 tiers, with tied tones sharing a tier) to pick a split. Each
respondent gets the first rule below that applies:

1. **All four tones tied (straightliner):** Self efficacy 40%, Value affirmation 20%, Legitimizing 20%, Norms 20%.
2. **Norms in the highest tier:** Self efficacy 30%, Norms 30%, Value affirmation 20%, Legitimizing 20%.
3. **Self efficacy and Value affirmation in the same tier:** 40% each, Legitimizing 20%, Norms dropped.
4. **Value affirmation in a higher tier than Self efficacy:** Value affirmation 50%, Self efficacy 25%, Legitimizing 25%, Norms dropped.
5. **Self efficacy in a higher tier than Value affirmation:** Self efficacy 50%, Value affirmation 25%, Legitimizing 25%, Norms dropped.

```{r}
#| label: Data-Driven Method
weights_data_driven <- data_driven_weights(pref_by_tone)

panel_data_driven <- weighted_method(
  weights_data_driven, "Data-driven", "dodgerblue4", "data_driven_rating")

plot_rating_hist(panel_data_driven, "data_driven_rating",
                 "Data-driven: drop Acknowledging, preference-based split of the other four tones",
                 fill = "dodgerblue4")

# Number of preference tiers among the four remaining tones
pref_by_tone |>
  filter(tone != "acknowledging") |>
  drop_na(pref) |>
  summarise(n_tiers = n_distinct(pref), .by = subid) |>
  count(n_tiers, name = "respondents")

# Respondents per rule
rule_counts <- weights_data_driven |>
  distinct(subid, rule) |>
  count(rule, name = "respondents") |>
  mutate(pct = respondents / sum(respondents))
rule_counts

# Do the rules' premises hold? Mean rating of each remaining tone within each rule group
tone_means |>
  filter(tone != "acknowledging") |>
  inner_join(distinct(weights_data_driven, subid, rule), by = "subid") |>
  summarise(mean_rating = mean(rating), .by = c(rule, tone)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = tone, values_from = mean_rating) |>
  left_join(rule_counts, by = "rule")

# Compared with the fixed 40/40/20 split (no individualization) and the best case
compare_methods(top = panel_3tone_weighted, mid = panel_data_driven, bot = panel_best)

method_tracker <- method_tracker |>
  track_method(panel_data_driven, weights = weights_data_driven)

method_tracker
```
